standfirst: A caregiver who has never once been cared for, his autistic brother, and a children's author with no idea how to be a person. It looked like a fairy tale and played like a case study. These six are about the same thing: what it costs to look after someone, and who is supposed to look after you.

picks.why: The direct ancestor. Noh Hee-kyung wrote mental illness as weather rather than as a twist six years earlier, with a psychiatrist and a novelist under one roof and a household of walking wounded around them. Same conviction that treatment is unglamorous and ongoing. Difference: no fairy-tale visual layer, and the romance is more central.

An autistic-coded young man and the reluctant adult who becomes responsible for him, doing work nobody else will do. Everything Moon Sang-tae's storyline was reaching for, given ten full episodes instead of a subplot. Difference: zero romance, and it is structured as case-of-the-week grief.

Caregiving from the other end of a life: a seventy-year-old learning ballet and a broke young dancer who did not ask to be needed. Same insistence that being looked after is not shameful. Difference: quiet and small where this was operatic, and it will hollow you out gently rather than loudly.

A whole town of adults with untreated wounds, told in chapters so each one gets its own hour. If what you valued was the show's refusal to make anyone's damage decorative, this does it across ten people. Difference: no single protagonist to attach to, and no clinical framing at all.

Runs on the same fable logic: a bright surface, an unreliable frame, and a reveal that makes you rewatch everything you just laughed at. Difference: the reframe is the whole point, so it plays as a puzzle first and an ache second.

Pure aftercare. Medicine as ordinary kindness, no villains, nobody's trauma weaponised. Watch it if the last three episodes left you raw. Difference: almost no tension, which after this show is the feature.

against.title: Extraordinary Attorney Woo
against.why: The reflex pick because of the neurodivergent lead, and it is a lovely show. But it is a sunny weekly procedural where the lead's difference is mostly a superpower. This show is about a family being ground down. Not the same contract.

against.title: Kill Me, Heal Me
against.why: Suggested for the psychiatric premise. It plays dissociative identity as a romantic-comedy device with a costume change per personality. Charming, entirely unserious about the illness.

against.title: Crash Landing on You
against.why: The default comfort pick. It is comfort, and this show is not, and after Ko Mun-yeong the tonal gearshift is jarring rather than restful.
